newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq said to endanger U.N. helicopter flights.
newsitem.headline: Iraq said to endanger U.N. helicopter flights.

text.p: Iraq physically interfered with four U.N. helicopter flights last week, forcing the end to U.N. arms inspection missions, the Security Council was told on Tuesday.

Council President Sergei Lavrov of Russia said the council would discuss the matter behind closed doors on Wednesday after being briefed by Rolf Ekeus, chief of the U.N. special commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.
Lavrov also said he would call in Iraq's U.N. envoy, Nizar Hamdoon.

In a letter to the council, Ekeus said: "In the last few days, there have been four serious incidents in which the lives of the crews of the commission's helicopters and the aircraft themselves were endangered through the actions of the Iraqi air personnel on board the aircraft or through the manoeuvres of the accompanying Iraqi helicopter.
"These actions resulted in the air missions having to be terminated without successfully carrying out their tasks."

Ekeus, who has frequently complained of Iraqi efforts to block U.N. weapons teams, said helicopter flights were an integral part of inspection missions. They ensured that no Iraqi personnel, vehicles or aircraft left the sites before they could be inspected by U.N. ground teams.
He did not disclose the locations of the four incidents or say what Iraqi facilities were being inspected.
UNSCOM uses five helicopters in Iraq provided by Chile, along with some 40 Chilean officers to man and service them.

In the first incident on June 4, Ekeus said, "The Iraqi air personnel threatened to shut off the fuel pump and physically manhandled the chief air inspector and the commission's photographer in order to prevent them from taking photographs of the inspection site, including the departure from the site of two Iraqi helicopters."

In the second incident on June 5, "One of the Iraqi personnel, among other actions, grabbed the co-pilot's control (cyclic stick) shaking it very violently, leading the commission's pilot to immediately abort the mission and to return to his base," he said.

Ekeus said in the third incident on June 7 an accompanying Iraqi helicopter "placed itself in the path of the commission's aircraft, causing the commission's pilot to make a radical manoeuvre to avoid a dangerous situation."

Subsequently, one of the Iraqi personnel aboard that U.N. craft interfered with the controls, resulting in a "temporary deviation from controlled flight." The Iraqi said he would "do whatever he could to stop the aircraft flying and indicated that he was acting under orders," Ekeus added.

In the fourth incident, also on June 7, an accompanying Iraqi helicopter flew alongside, but slightly higher than the U.N. craft, "so close that its main rotor overlapped the rotor of the commission's aircraft by some eight feet" (about two meters). An Iraqi on board said he would not order the Iraqi helicopter to move away as he had orders from Baghdad.

"All these incidents appeared to have been motivated by a determination on the Iraqi side not to permit the commission to operate its aircraft in the neighbourhood of areas which Iraq considered to be 'sensitive' or 'diplomatic' sites despite the fact that those sites were under ground inspection where access was permitted," Ekeus said.
After being called in later by the president of the Security Council, Iraqi U.N. envoy Nizar Hamdoon told reporters he would obtain further information Baghdad.
"But it all reminds me of the Hollywood fiction movies," he said, "as if somebody of the Iraqi staff is becoming suicidal, trying to kill himself with the others."

Iraq "obviously has frustration about the way the (U.N.) commission has been running those flights in recent days," he added. One of the incidents occurred during a planned inspection of a university in the Tikrit area -- President Saddam Husein's home town north of Baghdad -- when the U.N. pilot "insisted on flying over a presidential site, which is sensitive," even though he could have taken a more direct route, Hamdoon said.
